name: C++
description: A high-performance, systems-level language with manual memory control and powerful abstractions via the STL.

modules.title: Syntax Basics, Variables & Data Types

pages.title: Anatomy of a C++ Program
Memory, Sizes & Initialization Forms
pages.markdown:
## How Big Is a Variable, Really?

C++ lets you ask the compiler directly with the `sizeof` operator:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    cout << sizeof(int) << endl;       // typically 4 bytes
    cout << sizeof(double) << endl;    // typically 8 bytes
    cout << sizeof(char) << endl;      // always 1 byte
    cout << sizeof(bool) << endl;      // typically 1 byte
    return 0;
}
```

These sizes are not guaranteed by the standard to be identical on every platform — only minimum ranges are guaranteed — but on essentially all modern desktop/mobile platforms `int` is 4 bytes and `double` is 8 bytes. This matters because it directly determines the range of values a type can hold: a 4-byte signed `int` can represent roughly -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. Push past that range (**integer overflow**) and signed overflow is technically **undefined behavior** — in practice it usually wraps around, but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, which can produce surprising optimizations.

## Three Ways to Initialize

C++ has accumulated three syntaxes for initializing a variable, and they are not fully interchangeable:

```cpp
int a = 5;      // copy initialization
int b(5);       // direct initialization
int c{5};       // brace (uniform) initialization — C++11+
```

Brace initialization is the modern recommendation because it catches **narrowing conversions** at compile time:

```cpp
int d = 3.9;    // compiles silently, d becomes 3 (data loss!)
int e{3.9};     // ERROR: narrowing conversion, won't compile
```

That single difference makes `{}` initialization noticeably safer for catching accidental precision loss, which is why style guides increasingly favor it for new code.

## Type Deduction with `auto`

Since C++11, `auto` asks the compiler to figure out a variable's type from its initializer:

```cpp
auto count = 10;        // deduced as int
auto ratio = 3.14;      // deduced as double
auto label = string("x"); // deduced as std::string
```

`auto` does not make C++ dynamically typed — the type is still fixed at compile time, it's just written for you. It becomes especially valuable later with iterators and templates, where spelling out the real type name would be long and brittle. One nuance worth knowing early: `auto` strips references and top-level `const` by default (`auto x = someConstRef;` gives you a plain, mutable copy), so when you want to preserve those qualities you write `const auto&` or `auto&` explicitly.

pages.title: const-Correctness, Naming & Common Pitfalls
pages.markdown:
## const-Correctness

The `const` keyword marks a variable as unmodifiable after initialization:

```cpp
const double PI = 3.14159;
PI = 3.0; // compile error: assignment of read-only variable
```

Using `const` liberally is a hallmark of good C++ style: it documents intent ("this value never changes"), lets the compiler catch accidental mutation, and — for parameters — enables the compiler to make certain optimizations. You'll see it constantly on function parameters (`const string& name`) once references are introduced.

## Naming Conventions

C++ doesn't enforce a naming style, but conventions matter for readability across a team:

- Variables and functions: `snake_case` (`total_score`) or `camelCase` (`totalScore`) — pick one and stay consistent within a codebase.
- Constants and macros: often `ALL_CAPS` (`MAX_SIZE`).
- Types (classes, structs): `PascalCase` (`BankAccount`).
- Avoid single-letter names outside of tight loop counters (`i`, `j`) or extremely short-lived scratch variables.

## Common Pitfalls

**Uninitialized locals contain garbage.** Unlike some languages, C++ does not automatically zero-initialize local variables of fundamental types:

```cpp
int x;              // x holds whatever bits were already in that memory
cout << x << endl;  // undefined value — could print anything
```

Always initialize variables at the point of declaration (`int x = 0;`) unless you have a specific reason not to.

**Silent narrowing with `=`.** As shown above, `int n = 3.9;` compiles and quietly truncates to `3`. Prefer `{}` initialization when you want the compiler to flag this.

**Signed/unsigned comparisons.** Comparing a signed and unsigned integer implicitly converts the signed one to unsigned, which can produce surprising results for negative numbers:

```cpp
int a = -1;
unsigned int b = 1;
if (a < b) cout << "a is smaller\n"; // does NOT print! -1 becomes huge unsigned
```

Modern compilers warn about this (`-Wsign-compare`); pay attention to those warnings rather than suppressing them.

**Integer overflow.** `int` arithmetic that exceeds the type's range is undefined behavior for signed types. If you need very large counts, reach for `long long` or an unsigned type when negativity truly can't occur, and consider whether a computation might exceed 2 billion well before it actually does.

modules.title: Operators, Expressions & Type Conversion

pages.title: Arithmetic, Relational & Logical Operators
pages.markdown:
C++'s operator set will feel immediately familiar if you know C, Java, or JavaScript — it's one of the language families that shaped those others.

## Arithmetic Operators

```cpp
int a = 7, b = 2;
cout << a + b << endl;  // 9
cout << a - b << endl;  // 5
cout << a * b << endl;  // 14
cout << a / b << endl;  // 3  (integer division truncates)
cout << a % b << endl;  // 1  (remainder)
```

`++` and `--` increment/decrement by one, in both prefix (`++x`) and postfix (`x++`) forms. The difference matters when the result is used immediately: prefix increments *then* returns the new value; postfix returns the *old* value and increments afterward.

```cpp
int x = 5;
cout << x++ << endl; // prints 5, x is now 6
cout << ++x << endl; // x becomes 7, prints 7
```

## Relational Operators

`== != < > <= >=` compare two values and produce a `bool`. Nothing exotic here, except that comparing floating-point numbers with `==` is risky (covered on the pitfalls page).

## Logical Operators

`&&` (AND), `||` (OR), and `!` (NOT) combine boolean expressions and **short-circuit**: in `a() && b()`, if `a()` returns `false`, `b()` is never called, because the overall result is already determined. This is not just an optimization — code routinely relies on it for safety:

```cpp
int* p = nullptr;
if (p != nullptr && *p > 0) { /* safe: *p only evaluated if p is non-null */ }
```

Don't confuse `&&`/`||` with `&`/`|`, which are **bitwise** operators that operate on the individual bits of integers and do not short-circuit:

```cpp
cout << (5 & 3) << endl; // 1  (0101 & 0011 = 0001)
cout << (5 | 3) << endl; // 7  (0101 | 0011 = 0111)
```

## Precedence and Parentheses

C++ follows standard mathematical precedence (`*`/`/`/`%` before `+`/`-`, comparisons before logical operators), but when an expression mixes several operator families it's almost always more readable — and safer — to add explicit parentheses rather than rely on memorized precedence tables.

pages.title: Implicit Conversions & the Usual Arithmetic Rules
pages.markdown:
## Integer Division Truncates

When both operands of `/` are integers, the result is an integer — the fractional part is discarded (truncated toward zero, not rounded):

```cpp
cout << 7 / 2 << endl;   // 3, not 3.5
cout << -7 / 2 << endl;  // -3, truncation is toward zero
```

## Type Promotion in Mixed Expressions

When an expression mixes types, C++ applies the **usual arithmetic conversions**: the "smaller" or "less precise" operand is implicitly promoted to match the "larger" one before the operation happens.

```cpp
int a = 7;
double b = 2.0;
cout << a / b << endl; // a is promoted to double first: 3.5
```

The general hierarchy (simplified) is: `bool`/`char` → `int` → `long` → `long long` → `float` → `double` → `long double`. Whenever one operand in a binary operation is "further right" in that chain, the other is silently converted to match before the operation executes.

This silent promotion is convenient but can hide bugs. A classic example:

```cpp
int total = 7, count = 2;
double average = total / count;      // BUG: int/int = 3, THEN converted to 3.0
double correct = (double)total / count; // 3.5, converts before dividing
```

Notice the difference is not in the type of the *result variable* (`double average` in both cases) but in *when* the conversion happens — the division itself must involve a floating-point operand for the fractional part to survive.

## Explicit Conversion with static_cast

`static_cast<T>(value)` is the modern, explicit way to convert between related types:

```cpp
int a = 7, b = 2;
cout << static_cast<double>(a) / b << endl; // 3.5
```

Compared to the old C-style cast `(double)a`, `static_cast` states exactly what kind of conversion is intended and is checked more strictly by the compiler (it will refuse conversions that don't make sense, like casting a pointer to an unrelated struct type), which is why style guides ban C-style casts in modern C++ code.

## Overflow During Promotion

Promotion protects against precision loss in the "widening" direction (`int` to `double`) but not overflow in the other direction. Assigning a `double` back into an `int`, or a `long long` into an `int`, truncates or wraps without warning unless you've enabled and are heeding compiler narrowing diagnostics.

pages.title: Casts, Pitfalls & Floating-Point Comparison
pages.markdown:
## The Four Named Casts

Modern C++ deliberately splits the vague C-style cast `(T)x` into four distinct, searchable operators:

- **`static_cast<T>(x)`** — everyday conversions between related types (`int` ↔ `double`, base ↔ derived pointer with a known relationship). Use this by default.
- **`const_cast<T>(x)`** — adds or removes `const`/`volatile`. Rare, and a sign you should question the design if you need it.
- **`reinterpret_cast<T>(x)`** — reinterprets raw bits (e.g., pointer to an unrelated type). Low-level, dangerous, and rare in application code.
- **`dynamic_cast<T>(x)`** — a runtime-checked cast down a polymorphic class hierarchy (requires `virtual` functions); returns `nullptr` (for pointers) if the cast is invalid.

Avoiding the old C-style cast is a strong convention in modern C++: `static_cast` etc. are easy to `grep` for and make the *intent* of a conversion visible in code review, whereas `(T)x` silently picks whichever of the four behaviors applies and hides potentially dangerous reinterpretations.

## Comparing Signed and Unsigned

```cpp
int a = -1;
unsigned int b = 1;
if (a < b) { /* unreachable! */ }
```

Because `a` is implicitly converted to `unsigned int` before the comparison, `-1` becomes a very large positive number (due to how two's-complement wraps), so `a < b` is `false`. Enable and respect `-Wsign-compare` warnings, and avoid mixing signed and unsigned types in the same comparison where possible — prefer signed integers for counts that might need to represent "not found" as `-1`.

## Floating-Point Equality Is a Trap

```cpp
double x = 0.1 + 0.2;
if (x == 0.3) { /* often FALSE! */ }
```

Floating-point numbers cannot exactly represent most decimal fractions in binary, so `0.1 + 0.2` typically evaluates to something like `0.30000000000000004`. Never compare floating-point values with `==`; instead compare against a small tolerance (**epsilon**):

```cpp
#include <cmath>
bool nearlyEqual = std::fabs(x - 0.3) < 1e-9;
```

## A Practical Rule of Thumb

When you find yourself reaching for a cast, pause and ask: is this converting between numeric types I control (`static_cast` is fine), or am I fighting the type system to work around a design problem? Casts are a tool, not something to sprinkle defensively — each one is a small promise to the compiler that you know more than it does, and that promise should be true.

modules.title: Arrays, Strings & the STL

pages.title: C-Style Arrays, std::string & std::vector
pages.markdown:
## C-Style Arrays

A C-style array is a fixed-size, contiguous block of elements of the same type:

```cpp
int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
cout << arr[0] << endl;   // 10
cout << arr[4] << endl;   // 50
```

Its size is fixed at compile time (or at allocation time for a dynamic array) and, crucially, **the array itself does not know its own length** — `arr` decays to a pointer to its first element as soon as you pass it to a function, losing the size information entirely. This is exactly the kind of footgun the STL was designed to eliminate.

## std::string

Unlike Python or Java, where strings are immutable, `std::string` (from `<string>`) is a mutable, growable sequence of characters:

```cpp
#include <string>
string s = "hello";
s += ", world";        // mutates s in place
s[0] = 'H';            // direct character mutation
cout << s << endl;     // "Hello, world"
cout << s.length() << endl; // 12
```

`std::string` manages its own memory internally (it's really a small class wrapping a dynamically-sized character buffer), so you never call `new`/`delete` for it yourself.

## std::vector

`std::vector<T>` (from `<vector>`) is the STL's dynamic array — the default container to reach for whenever you need a resizable sequence:

```cpp
#include <vector>
vector<int> nums = {5, 3, 1, 4, 2};
nums.push_back(6);          // append
cout << nums.size() << endl; // 6
cout << nums[0] << endl;     // 5
```

Like a C-array, elements are stored contiguously in memory, but unlike a C-array, `vector` tracks its own size and automatically grows its internal buffer as needed via `push_back`.

## Algorithms Operate on Iterator Ranges

`<algorithm>` provides generic functions that work across any STL container via a pair of **iterators** marking a `[begin, end)` range:

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());              // ascending sort
auto it = find(nums.begin(), nums.end(), 4); // iterator to first 4, or end()
int total = accumulate(nums.begin(), nums.end(), 0); // from <numeric>
```

Because these functions work on iterator ranges rather than a specific container type, the same `sort` works on a `vector<int>`, a `vector<string>`, or even a plain C-array (via pointer "iterators" `arr, arr + 5`).

pages.title: How vector Grows & How string Avoids Allocating
Bounds Checking, Iterator Invalidation & Algorithm Idioms
pages.markdown:
## operator[] vs. at()

Both index into a `vector` or `string`, but they behave very differently on an out-of-range index:

```cpp
vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3};
cout << v[10];      // undefined behavior — may crash, may return garbage, may "work"
cout << v.at(10);   // throws std::out_of_range — a catchable, well-defined error
```

`operator[]` skips bounds checking entirely for speed, matching C-array semantics. `at()` checks and throws. A common idiom: use `[]` in hot, already-validated loops where you control the index, and `at()` when the index comes from external/untrusted input and you want a safe failure mode instead of silent corruption.

## The Erase-Remove Idiom

Removing elements from a `vector` while iterating it is a classic footgun (covered in the Control Flow module). The standard, safe pattern for "remove all elements matching a condition" is:

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};
v.erase(remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(),
                   [](int n) { return n % 2 == 0; }),
        v.end());
// v is now {1, 3, 5}
```

`remove_if` doesn't actually shrink the vector — it shuffles the "kept" elements to the front and returns an iterator marking the new logical end; `erase` then actually deletes the leftover tail. This two-step "remove, then erase" dance is idiomatic enough that it has a name (erase-remove idiom) precisely because a beginner's first instinct — erasing elements one at a time inside a range-`for` loop — invalidates iterators and is undefined behavior.

## Choosing the Right Container

- Need indexed, contiguous, resizable storage? **`vector`** — the default choice.
- Need fast lookup by key, sorted iteration? **`map`**.
- Need fast lookup by key, don't care about order? **`unordered_map`**.
- Need to reject duplicates, keep things sorted? **`set`**.
- Need fast insertion/removal at both ends, not the middle? **`deque`**.

## Common Pitfalls

- Forgetting a C-array "decays" to a pointer when passed to a function, losing its length — prefer `vector` or pass the length explicitly.
- Using `[]` on user-supplied indices without validating range first.
- Holding a reference/pointer/iterator into a `vector` across an operation that might reallocate it.
- Comparing `string`s or containers with `==` works element-wise as expected — but comparing raw C-strings (`char*`) with `==` compares *pointers*, not contents, a frequent trap when mixing C-style and C++-style strings.

modules.title: Error Handling

pages.title: try, catch & throw
Stack Unwinding, Catching by Reference & RAII
When (Not) to Use Exceptions, and noexcept
pages.markdown:
## Exceptions Are for Exceptional, Not Routine, Conditions

A common design mistake is using exceptions for ordinary control flow — e.g., throwing to signal "value not found" in a lookup that's expected to miss sometimes. Exceptions carry real runtime cost (even when not thrown, they can inhibit some optimizations; when thrown, unwinding is comparatively expensive) and, more importantly, they obscure control flow for a case that isn't actually unusual. Prefer:

- A sentinel/optional return (`std::optional<T>`, or an iterator equal to `end()`) for "might not find it."
- A `bool` success flag or error code for expected, recoverable failure paths.
- Exceptions for genuinely exceptional situations: corrupted input, a failed resource acquisition, a violated precondition that indicates a bug.

```cpp
#include <optional>
optional<int> findIndex(const vector<int>& v, int target) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); i++)
        if (v[i] == target) return i;
    return nullopt; // "not found" is routine, not exceptional
}
```

## noexcept

A function can be marked `noexcept` to promise it will never throw:

```cpp
double square(double x) noexcept { return x * x; }
```

This is more than documentation: if a `noexcept` function *does* throw (perhaps by calling something that unexpectedly throws), the program calls `std::terminate` immediately rather than unwinding further — so the promise must be genuinely true. `noexcept` also matters for performance: some STL operations (like `vector`'s reallocation) will *move* elements instead of copying them only if the type's move constructor is `noexcept`, since moving during an exception-unsafe operation could leave the vector in a corrupted state if a throw happened partway through.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Catching `...` (catch-all) and silently swallowing the error.** This hides bugs and makes debugging painful — at minimum log or rethrow.
- **Throwing from a destructor.** If a destructor throws while the stack is already unwinding due to another exception, `std::terminate` is called immediately — destructors should essentially never throw.
- **Forgetting that resources acquired with raw `new`/manual APIs (not RAII wrappers) leak on the exception path** unless you add explicit `try`/`catch`/cleanup around every risky operation — another reason to prefer RAII wrappers (`unique_ptr`, `ifstream`, `lock_guard`) over manual resource management, covered further in the Pointers module.
- **Catching by value** instead of `const&`, which copies and slices derived exception types.

modules.title: Pointers & Manual Memory Management

pages.title: Pointers, Addresses & the Heap
pages.markdown:
## What a Pointer Is

A pointer is a variable that stores a **memory address** rather than a value directly:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int x = 42;
    int* p = &x;     // p holds the address of x
    cout << x << endl;    // 42
    cout << p << endl;    // some address, e.g. 0x7ffee...
    cout << *p << endl;   // 42 — *p dereferences p, "follow the address"
    *p = 100;             // writes through the pointer
    cout << x << endl;    // 100 — x itself changed
    return 0;
}
```

`&` (address-of) takes a variable's address; `*` (dereference), applied to a pointer, accesses the value it points to. These are the same `&`/`*` symbols used for references and multiplication respectively — context (declaration vs. expression) tells the compiler which meaning applies.

## Stack vs. Heap

Ordinary local variables (`int x = 42;`) live on the **stack**: memory automatically managed as functions are called and return, extremely fast to allocate, but tied to the current scope's lifetime.

The **heap** is a separate memory region for allocations that need to outlive the function that created them, or whose size isn't known until runtime. You request heap memory explicitly with `new`, and must release it explicitly with `delete`:

```cpp
int* heapInt = new int(42);   // allocated on the heap
cout << *heapInt << endl;     // 42
delete heapInt;                // must free manually, exactly once
```

Every `new` must be matched by exactly one `delete` (or `delete[]` for arrays allocated with `new[]`). Forget it, and that memory is never reclaimed for the life of the program — a **memory leak**. Delete it twice, and you get undefined behavior (a **double-free**), often a crash.

## Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays

A pointer to an array's first element can be advanced like an index:

```cpp
int arr[3] = {10, 20, 30};
int* p = arr;         // arrays decay to a pointer to their first element
cout << *(p + 1) << endl; // 20 — same as arr[1]
```

This is exactly why C-style arrays "decay" to pointers when passed to functions (mentioned in the Arrays/STL module) — the array's length information is not part of the pointer, only the starting address is.

RAII & Smart Pointers: Managing Memory Automatically
pages.markdown:
## RAII: Tie Cleanup to Object Lifetime

**RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)** is C++'s core idiom for resource safety: acquire a resource in a constructor, release it in the destructor, and let the language's automatic destructor calls (at scope exit, whether by normal return *or* exception) guarantee cleanup happens exactly once, everywhere. Modern C++ almost never calls `new`/`delete` directly in application code — instead it wraps heap allocations in RAII types from `<memory>`.

## std::unique_ptr: Sole Ownership

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    auto p = make_unique<int>(42);   // heap int, owned solely by p
    cout << *p << endl;               // 42
    return 0;
}                                      // p's destructor runs automatically -> delete happens here
```

`unique_ptr` cannot be copied (copying would create two "owners" of the same memory, and two eventual deletes of the same address), only **moved**:

```cpp
unique_ptr<int> a = make_unique<int>(5);
unique_ptr<int> b = move(a);   // ownership transfers to b; a is now null
```

This makes ownership explicit and traceable in the type system: exactly one `unique_ptr` owns the object at any given time, and the compiler enforces it.

## std::shared_ptr: Shared Ownership via Reference Counting

```cpp
#include <memory>
auto a = make_shared<int>(10);
auto b = a;             // both a and b now own the same int; refcount = 2
cout << a.use_count() << endl; // 2
```

`shared_ptr` maintains an internal reference count; the underlying object is deleted only when the *last* `shared_ptr` pointing to it is destroyed. This is more flexible than `unique_ptr` but carries overhead (the refcount itself, and atomic increments/decrements for thread safety) — use `unique_ptr` by default and reach for `shared_ptr` only when genuinely shared ownership is needed.

## std::weak_ptr: Breaking Reference Cycles

Two `shared_ptr`s that reference each other (e.g., a parent and child pointing at one another) create a cycle that reference counting can never resolve to zero — a leak. `weak_ptr` observes a `shared_ptr`-managed object *without* contributing to its reference count, breaking such cycles; you must call `.lock()` to get a temporary `shared_ptr` before using it, which safely yields `nullptr` if the object has already been destroyed.

## The Rule of Three / Five, Briefly

If a class manually manages a resource (raw pointer, file handle), and you write a custom **destructor**, you almost always also need a custom **copy constructor** and **copy assignment operator** (the "Rule of Three") to avoid two objects double-freeing the same resource on copy — extended to five in modern C++ by also considering **move constructor/move assignment** for efficient ownership transfer. Wrapping the resource in a `unique_ptr`/`shared_ptr` member instead routinely lets you avoid writing any of these five by hand — the smart pointer's own correct Rule-of-Five implementation does the work for you, which is the biggest practical argument for preferring smart pointers over raw owning pointers.

keyTakeaways: A pointer stores an address; & takes an address, * dereferences a pointer.
Local variables live on the stack; new allocates on the heap and must be paired with exactly one delete (or delete[] for arrays).
Dereferencing a null or dangling pointer, or freeing memory twice, is undefined behavior.
RAII ties a resource's cleanup to an object's destructor, guaranteeing cleanup on every exit path including exceptions.
std::unique_ptr gives sole, move-only ownership and frees memory automatically when it goes out of scope.
std::shared_ptr gives reference-counted shared ownership; std::weak_ptr observes without owning, breaking reference cycles.
If a class manually owns a resource, it generally needs the Rule of Three/Five — wrapping the resource in a smart pointer usually avoids writing that boilerplate.
Prefer smart pointers (RAII) over raw new/delete in new code.

keyTakeaways: ifstream reads, ofstream writes, fstream does both; all three live in <fstream>.
File streams close automatically via RAII when they go out of scope, but always check success with if (!stream) after opening.
ios::app appends instead of truncating an existing file; ios::binary disables text-mode newline translation for exact byte I/O.
getline(stream, str) reads one line at a time from a file or string stream, and accepts a custom delimiter as a third argument.
stringstream/istringstream/ostringstream (<sstream>) reuse the familiar <</>> interface to parse or build strings in memory.
<algorithm>/<numeric> provide generic operations like sort, transform, accumulate, and max_element that work across containers.
<chrono> encodes time units in the type system (milliseconds, microseconds, etc.), preventing unit-confusion bugs in timing code.
